'''''Ulmus minor''''' <small>[[Philip Miller|Mill.]]</small>, the '''field elm''', is by far the most [[Polymorphism (biology)|polymorphic]] of the European species, although its taxonomy remains a matter of contention. Its natural range is predominantly south European, extending to [[Asia Minor]] and Iran; its northern outposts are the [[Baltic Sea|Baltic]] islands of [[Öland]] and [[Gotland]],<ref>[http://www.ulmen-handbuch.de/handbuch/ulmus/fotos/gattung_ulmus_02_gr.jpg ''Ulmus minor'' in Gotland, Sweden: ulmen-handbuch.de/handbuch/ulmus]</ref> although it may have been introduced by humans. The tree's typical habitat is low-lying forest along the main rivers, growing in association with [[oak]] and [[Fraxinus|ash]], where it tolerates summer floods as well as droughts.<ref name=Heybroek,1>Heybroek, H. M., Goudzwaard, L, Kaljee, H. (2009). ''Iep of olm, karakterboom van de Lage Landen'' (:Elm, a tree with character of the Low Countries). KNNV, Uitgeverij. {{ISBN|9789050112819}}</ref>

Current treatment of the species owes much to [[Richard Hook Richens|Richens]],<ref name=Richens1968>{{cite journal|doi=10.1002/fedr.19680790102 | last1 = Richens | first1 = R. H. | year = 1968 | title = The correct designation of the European field elms |journal=Feddes Repertorium |volume=79 |issue=1–2 |pages=1–2 }}</ref> who noted (1983) that several varieties of field elm are distinguishable on the European mainland. Of these, he listed the small-leaved ''U. minor'' of France and Spain; the narrow-leaved ''U. minor'' of northern and central Italy; the densely hairy leaved ''U. minor'' of southern Italy and Greece; the ''U. minor'' with small-toothed leaves from the Balkans; the ''U. minor'' with large-toothed leaves from the Danube region; and the small-leaved ''U. minor'' from southern Russia and Ukraine.<ref>Richens, R. H., ''Elm'' (Cambridge 1983), p.18</ref> As for British varieties, "the continental populations most closely related [to eastern English Field Elm] are in central Europe", while south-western forms were introduced from France.<ref>Richens, R. H., ''Elm'' (Cambridge 1983), p.21</ref> He concluded, however, that owing to incomplete field-research at the time of writing, it was "not possible to present an overall breakdown of the European Field Elm into regional varieties".<ref>Richens, R. H., ''Elm'' (Cambridge 1983), p.88</ref> The epithet 'red' elm was commonly used by British foresters, an allusion to the colour of the timber.<ref name=Edlin>Edlin, H. L. (1947). ''British Woodland Trees'',  p.26. 3rd. edition. London: B. T. Batsford Ltd.</ref>

Richens sank a number of British elms, notably [[English elm]], as either subspecies or varieties of ''U. minor'' in 1968. However, [[Ronald Melville (botanist)|Melville]],<ref name=Melville,a>{{cite journal | last1 = Melville | first1 = R | year = 1978 | title = On the discrimination of species in hybrid swarms with special reference to ''Ulmus'' and the nomenclature of ''U. minor'' (Mill.) and ''U. carpinifolia'' (Gled.) | journal = Taxon | volume = 27 | issue = 4 | pages = 345–351 | doi = 10.2307/1220370 | jstor = 1220370 }}</ref> writing ten years later, identified five distinct species (including [[Ulmus glabra|''U. glabra'']] in the count), several varieties and numerous complex hybrids.  In 1992 [[Jayne V. Armstrong|Armstrong]]<ref name=Armstrong>{{cite journal | last1 = Armstrong | first1 = J. V. | last2 = Sell | first2 = P. D. | year = 1996 | title = A revision of the British elms (''Ulmus'' L., Ulmaceae): the historical background | journal = Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society | volume = 120 | pages = 39–50 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.1996.tb00478.x|url =https://geoscience.net/ftxt.php?pdf=002742058|access-date=26 October 2017| doi-access = free | url-access = subscription }}</ref> identified no fewer than forty British species and microspecies. [[Clive Stace]] (1997) wrote of the British elms "The two-species (''glabra'' and ''minor'') concept of Richens is not sufficiently discriminating to be of taxonomic value". Nevertheless, it is Richens' classification which has been the most commonly adopted in recent years, although it is not used in ''Flora Europaea''.<ref>[http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/parent=/filename=feout/firstval=11/SID=484.1161948890?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Ulmus&SPECIES_XREF=&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= Flora Europaea]</ref><ref name=Stace>Stace, C. A. (1997). ''New Flora of the British Isles''. 2nd edition. Cambridge University Press.</ref>

In 2009 Dr Max Coleman of the [[Royal Botanic Garden, Edinburgh]] wrote: "The advent of DNA fingerprinting has shed considerable light on the question. A number of studies have now shown that the distinctive forms Melville elevated to species and Richens lumped together as field elm are single clones, all genetically identical, which have been propagated by vegetative means such as cuttings or root suckers. This means that enigmatic British elms such as [[Ulmus minor 'Plotii'|Plot elm]] and [[English elm]] have been shown to be single clones of field elm. Although Richens did not have the evidence to prove it, he was correct in recognising a series of clones and grouping them together as a variable species."<ref name="Max Coleman p. 22">Max Coleman, ed.: ''Wych Elm'' ([[Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh]] publication, 2009; {{ISBN|978-1-906129-21-7}}); p. 22</ref>

It is hoped that analysis of [[molecular marker]]s will ultimately eliminate the taxonomic confusion.

==Description==
The tree typically grows to < 30 m (98 ft) and bears a rounded crown.<ref>Photographs of ''Ulmus minor'' in France (L'orme de Martailly-lès-Brancion), krapooarboricole.wordpress.com [http://krapooarboricole.wordpress.com/category/arbres-coup-de-coeur/ormes/] ; in Portugal, 1.bp.blogspot.com [http://1.bp.blogspot.com/_S20HPrGKodc/SVJ-IqZGDyI/AAAAAAAAENA/1w0jVsk1zG0/s1600-h/ulmeiro1.JPG].</ref> The bark of the trunk is rough, furrowed lightly in older trees to form a block pattern. Young branchlets occasionally have corky wings. The shoots are slender compared with those of wych elm. The leaves are smaller than those of the other European species, hence the specific epithet ''minor'', however they can vary greatly according to the maturity of the tree. Leaves on juvenile growth (suckers, seedlings etc.) are coarse and pubescent, whereas those on mature growth are generally smooth, though remaining highly variable in form; there are generally fewer than 12 pairs of side veins.<ref>{{Naturalis Biodiversity Center |id=L.4222648 }} Labelled ''Ulmus carpinifolia'' <small>Gled.</small>, [[Pont du Gard]], France, 1981</ref> A common characteristic is the presence of minute black glands along the leaf veins, detectable with the aid of a magnifying glass.<ref name=Heybroek,1/>  The [[samara (fruit)|samarae]] are oval or obovate, glabrous, {{convert|12|–|15|mm|in|frac=32|abbr=on}} long, notched at the top, with the seed close to the notch.<ref name="Bean">Bean, W. J. (1981). ''Trees and shrubs hardy in Great Britain'', 7th edition. Murray, London. [http://beanstreesandshrubs.org/browse/ulmus/ulmus-carpinifolia-gleditsch/]</ref> ''Ulmus minor'' in France generally begins to flower and fruit when aged 10 years.<ref name="Brookes,b">Brookes, A. H. (2020). ''Great Fontley Elm Trial, 2020 Report''. Butterfly Conservation, Lulworth, England.</ref>

The species readily produces suckers from roots and stumps, even after devastation by [[Dutch elm disease]]; consequently genetic resources are not considered endangered.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.ipgri.cgiar.org/networks/euforgen/Networks/Noble_Hardwoods/Strategies/UlmusSppConsStrategy.htm | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030929123356/http://www.ipgri.cgiar.org/networks/euforgen/Networks/Noble_Hardwoods/Strategies/UlmusSppConsStrategy.htm | archive-date=2003-09-29 | title=European elms (Ulmus SPP.) genetic resources conservation strategy | access-date=2023-07-09 | url-status=live }}</ref>

==Pests and diseases==
The species has a hugely variable reaction to [[Dutch elm disease]] (DED), including all the fashionable pre-20th century plantsman's clones (see Subspecies and varieties). However, field elm is genetically highly variable; Italian specimens when inoculated with the pathogen displayed between 15 and 100% dieback and between 70 and 100% wilting.<ref name=Solla>Solla, A., Bohnens, J., Collin, E., Diamandis, S., Franke, A., Gil, L., Burón, M., Santini, A., Mittempergher, L., Pinon, J., Vanden Broeck, A. (2005). [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/229069171_Screening_European_Elms_for_resistance_to_Ophiostoma_novo-ulmi Screening European elms for resistance to Ophiostoma novo-ulmi]. ''Forest Science'', 51(2) 2005 134-141.</ref> 

Tolerance of [[elm yellows]] (phloem necrosis) is generally good, ''U. minor'' exhibiting symptoms such as the 'witch's broom' only sporadically throughout Italy, including [[Sicily]] and [[Sardinia]], however the disease was often locally common within the species in France, including [[Paris]].<ref name=Mittempergher>Mittempergher, L. (2000). Elm Yellows in Europe. in Dunn, C.P., (ed.): ''The Elms, Breeding, Conservation, & Disease Management.'' 104-105. Boston: Kluwer Academuic Publishing.</ref>

==Cultivation==
''U. minor'' in general and a number of clones in particular (see 'Cultivars' below) were once commonly cultivated across Europe in town and country, but owing to its susceptibility to Dutch elm disease, ''U. minor'' is now uncommon in cultivation. However, in an ongoing project that began in the 1990s, several thousand surviving field elms have been tested for innate resistance by national research institutes in the EU, with a view to returning field elm to cultivation.<ref name=Solla/> Results from Spain (2013), for example, confirm that a very small number of surviving field elms (about 0.5% of those tested) appear to have comparatively high levels of tolerance of the disease, and it is hoped that a controlled crossing of the best of these will produce resistant ''Ulmus minor'' hybrids for cultivation.<ref>[http://www.resistantelms.co.uk/spanish-clones/ 'Spanish Clones' (Oct. 2013) resistantelms.co.uk]</ref>

In the UK, despite its late leaf-flush in the north and its suckering habits, continental ''U. minor'' was occasionally planted as an ornamental urban tree. [[Augustine Henry]] wrote in 1913 that “In all probability many of” the ''U. minor'' planted in parks in Scotland were of French origin.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Elwes |first1=Henry John |last2=Henry |first2=Augustine |title=The Trees of Great Britain and Ireland, Volume VII |date=1913 |location=Edinburgh |isbn=978-1-108-06938-0 |page=1897–8 |url=https://archive.org/details/treesofgreatbrit07elweuoft/page/1897/mode/2up }}</ref> More recently ''U. minor'' seed was imported to the UK from Italy.<ref>E. E. Kemp (Curator, [[Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh]] 1950-71) in ''After the Elm'', eds. Clouston & Stansfield, (London, 1979)</ref> There are mature survivors in Edinburgh that are not the common ''U. minor'' cultivars (2015).<ref>Boswall Rd [two]; corner of Abbey Mount and Regent Rd; News Steps; Carlton Terrace Brae; Links Place; Seafield Place. Verified by samarae, leaves, suckering habit, form, and late leaf-flush; trees all on Streetview.</ref>

''U. minor'' was introduced, as ''U. campestris suberosa'' or simply ''U. suberosa'', to the US and Canada,<ref name=bobink>{{cite book|date=1902 |title=Bobbink and Atkins, Rutherford. N.J.|pages=50|url=https://archive.org/stream/CAT31285383#page/51/mode/2up}}</ref><ref name = Ottawa1899>{{Cite book|last1=Saunders|first1=William|last2=Macoun|first2=William Tyrrell|url=https://archive.org/stream/bulletinissues00ottogoog#page/n80/mode/2up/|title=Catalogue of the trees and shrubs in the arboretum and botanic gardens at the central experimental farm|year=1899|edition=2|pages=74–75|publisher=Ottawa }}</ref> where a few old specimens survive,<ref>[https://treesofvancouver.ca/field-elm/ Old ''U. minor'', field elm, 'Trees of Vancouver']</ref> and to the southern hemisphere, notably Australasia<ref>[https://trove.nla.gov.au/work/34926332?selectedversion=NBD9147128 Brookes, Margaret, & Barley, Richard, ''Plants listed in nursery catalogues in Victoria, 1855-1889'' (Ornamental Plant Collection Association, South Yarra, Victoria, 1992), p.303–304]</ref> and Argentina.<ref name = Hirsch>Hiersch, H., Hensen, I., Zalapa, J. Guries, R. & Brunet, J. (2013). Is hybridization a necessary condition for the evolution of invasiveness in non-native Siberian elm? ''Abstracts. Third International Elm Conference 2013. The elm after 100 years of Dutch elm disease''. Florence,  p.45. [http://elm2013.ipp.cnr.it/downloads/book_of_abstracts.pdf Abstract].</ref>

==Notable trees==
''U. minor'' can live to a great age. An ancient field elm stood until recently in the village square of [[Metaxades]], [[Thrace]], Greece. Having abandoned their original village in 1286 after cholera outbreaks, the villagers re-founded it in the hills where a young elm was growing beside a spring. An elm (reputedly the original) and the fountain were the focal-point of the village until the late 20th century.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://gym-metax.evr.sch.gr/dimos_metaxadon/metax_history.htm |title=Η ιστορία των Μεταξάδων |access-date=2010-12-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721083036/http://gym-metax.evr.sch.gr/dimos_metaxadon/metax_history.htm |archive-date=2011-07-21 }}</ref> The tallest recorded field elms in Greece were two specimens planted in 1650 beside the newly built church of the Archangels Michael and Gabriel, in Omali Voiou (Oμαλή Bοΐου) near [[Siatista]], which, despite being open-grown trees, attained a height of 40 metres by the mid-20th century.<ref>The elms of Omali Voiou: «Oι εκκλησίες της Oμαλής Bοΐου» [:The Churches of Omali Voiou], photograph 7 (p.25): www.scribd.com [https://www.scribd.com/doc/112445341/%CE%BF%CE%B9-%CE%B5%CE%BA%CE%BA%CE%BB%CE%B7%CF%83%CE%AF%CE%B5%CF%82-%CF%84%CE%B7%CF%82-%CE%BF%CE%BC%CE%B1%CE%BB%CE%AE%CF%82-%CE%B2%CE%BF%CE%90%CE%BF%CF%85]</ref> The immemorial elm opposite the village square of Aidona in [[Thessaly]], Greece<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20140506172652/https://sites.google.com/site/prostateuomenespertrikalwn/prostateuomenes-perioches-periphereiakes-enotetas-trikalon/diateretea-mnemeia-physes/phtelia-tes-aedonas-kalampakas Summer photograph of the centuries-old Aidona elm: sites.google.com]</ref><ref>[http://nikos-manitarielassonas.blogspot.co.uk/2011/02/blog-post.html Winter photograph of Aidona elm: nikos-manitarielassonas, photograph 3]</ref> which has been "listed" as a national "Monument of Nature",<ref>''Διατηρητέα Μνημεία της Φύσεως'' αριθ.36 (:Listed Monuments of Nature, No. 36): https://web.archive.org/web/20080616173320/http://users.otenet.gr/~theonik/peribal/esthitik.htm</ref> lost its crown in a recent storm (2009) and has now been pollarded; it is regenerating vigorously. A rare example of a centuries-old field elm that retains its heartwood and crown is the 360-year-old specimen in the village square of Strinylas, [[Corfu]].<ref>[http://www.greeka.com/ionian/corfu/corfu-pictures/strinilas-pictures/members-1.htm The elm in Strinylas, Corfu: greeka.com]</ref><ref>The elm in Strinylas, Corfu: greeka.com/ionian/corfu/corfu-villages/strinilas-corfu.htm; https://web.archive.org/web/20011224222535/http://www.manfred-peters.de/Titel_Korfu_Tip_Nord.htm</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20181216031550/http://static.panoramio.com/photos/original/19585616.jpg The elm in Strinylas, Corfu: static.panoramio.com]</ref>

A tree said to be of similar age named [[The Old Elm]] (200 cm d.b.h.) still stands (2013) in the city of [[Sliven]], Bulgaria; other veterans are said to survive in the village of [[Samuilovo, Blagoevgrad Province|Samuilovo]], 7 km from Sliven.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Panoramio - Photo of The old Elm in Sliven (Ulmus kampestris) - more than 1 000 years old / Стария сливенски бряст / © by * Rosi * |url=http://www.panoramio.com/photo/98111069 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140111131358/http://www.panoramio.com/photo/98111069 |archive-date=2014-01-11 |access-date=2025-06-12 |website=www.panoramio.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://bnr.bg/sites/en/Lifestyle/ScienceAndNature/Pages/030114TheSlivenelmtree.aspx |title='The Sliven elm-tree runs for European Tree of the Year', bnr.bg |access-date=2014-01-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140111201713/http://bnr.bg/sites/en/Lifestyle/ScienceAndNature/Pages/030114TheSlivenelmtree.aspx |archive-date=2014-01-11 }}</ref>

In France, a tree reputedly over 650 years old survived in the centre of [[Biscarrosse]] south of [[Bordeaux]] until the summer of 2010, when it finally succumbed to Dutch elm disease.<ref>krapooarboricole.wordpress.com, [http://krapooarboricole.wordpress.com/2008/02/05/lorme-multi-seculaire-de-biscarosse-40/] [http://www.sudouest.fr/2010/08/28/l-orme-legendaire-171211-3307.php]  [http://www.pijouls.com/albums/alblormedebiscarrosse/page_01.htm]</ref> Another veteran with a 6-metre girth survives at [[Bettange]], France, close to the Belgian border, reputedly planted in 1593.<ref>arbresvenerables.free.fr {{cite web |title=Venerable Trees of the Earth - France |url=http://arbresvenerables.free.fr/ArbresVenerables/France%20GB.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080502060022/http://arbresvenerables.free.fr/ArbresVenerables/France%20GB.htm |archive-date=2008-05-02 |access-date=2015-02-05}}, krapooarboricole.wordpress.com [http://krapooarboricole.wordpress.com/category/arbres-coup-de-coeur/ormes/page/2/]</ref> Other wrecks include 'l'ormeau de Sully' in [[Villesèquelande]] near [[Carcassonne]],<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20171007021653/http://www.panoramio.com/photo/9735222 L'Ormeau de Sully, Villesèquelande, panoramio.com]</ref> "a magnificent tree supported by three metal props", said to have been planted in the early 17th C by the [[Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully|Duc de Sully]],<ref>sullystrees.weebly.com/list-of-trees-by-french-departements.html</ref>

A tree approximately 400 years old and 5.55 metres in girth grows in the town of [[Mergozzo]] in [[Piedmont]], Italy. 'L'olmo di Mergozzo', like its French counterparts 'l'orme de Biscarosse' and 'l'orme de Bettange', is hollowed out by age, its life prolonged by lopping, while in Spain the elm in the Plaza del Olmo ("Elm square" in Spanish) in [[Navajas]], [[Valencia]], is 6.3 metres in girth; planted in 1636 it features on the town crest.<ref>[http://www.navajas.es/portal/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=6&Itemid=7 Ayuntamiento de Navajas, Historia y patrimonio]</ref>

In England, large specimens once identified as ''U. minor'' subsp. ''minor'', the narrow- or smooth-leafed elm, were once commonplace in the eastern counties before the advent of DED. The largest recorded tree in the UK grew at [[Great Amwell]], [[Hertfordshire]],  measuring 40 m in height and 228 cm [[d.b.h.]] in 1911.<ref name=Elwes>{{cite book |last1=Elwes |first1=Henry John |last2=Henry |first2=Augustine |title=The Trees of Great Britain and Ireland, Volume VII |date=1913 |location=Edinburgh |isbn=978-1-108-06938-0 |page=1899 |url=https://archive.org/details/treesofgreatbrit07elweuoft/page/1898/mode/2up?q=amwell |access-date=15 December 2021}}</ref> Another famous specimen was the great elm that towered above its two siblings at the bottom of Long Melford Green, [[Long Melford]], Suffolk,<ref>Photograph of the great elms on Long Melford Green (Francis Frith Collection, images.francisfrith.com) [http://images.francisfrith.com/c10/450/39/L101004.jpg]</ref> till the group succumbed to disease in 1978. The three "were survivors of a former clone of at least nine elms, one dating from 1757".<ref>Photograph, plate XXI(h), in [[Oliver Rackham]], ''A History of the Countryside'' (London, 1986),  p.236.</ref> The Long Melford elms were painted in 1940 by the watercolourist [[Stanley Roy Badmin|S. R. Badmin]] in his 'Long Melford Green on a Frosty Morning', now in the [[Victoria and Albert Museum]].<ref>S. R. Badmin's 'Long Melford Green on a Frosty Morning', Victoria and Albert Museum [https://web.archive.org/web/20110803223448/http://www.vam.ac.uk/users/node/16047]</ref> The largest known surviving trees in England are at [[East Coker]], [[Somerset]] (30 m high, 95 cm [[d.b.h.]]), Termitts Farm near [[Hatfield Peverel]], [[Essex]] (25 m high, 145 d.b.h.), and [[Melchbourne]], [[Bedfordshire]], (147 cm d.b.h.).<ref name=Tree>{{Cite web |url=http://www.treeregister.org/treecollections/ |title=Tree Register Of the British Isles (TROBI) |access-date=2014-12-10 |archive-date=2014-12-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141215205710/http://www.treeregister.org/treecollections/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Subspecies, varieties, and former species sunk as ''U. minor''==
===England===
The name [[Ulmus minor subsp. minor|''Ulmus minor'' subsp. ''minor'']] was used by R. H. Richens<ref name = Richens280/> for field elm that was not [[Ulmus minor 'Atinia'|English elm]], [[Ulmus minor 'Stricta'|Cornish elm]], [[Ulmus minor 'Plotii'|Plot elm]] or [[Ulmus minor 'Sarniensis'|Guernsey elm]]. Many publications, however, continue to use plain ''Ulmus minor'' for undifferentiated field elm; indeed Dr Max Coleman of Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh argued in his 2002 paper 'British Elms' that there was no clear distinction between species and subspecies.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Coleman | first1 = M | year = 2002 | title = British elms | journal = British Wildlife | volume = 13 | issue = 6| pages = 390–395 }}</ref> Some authorities, among them Richens<ref>Richens, R. H., ''Elm'' (Cambridge, 1983)</ref> and Coleman,<ref name="Max Coleman p. 22"/> include [[Ulmus minor 'Atinia'|English elm]] among varieties of field elm, Richens calling English elm ''U. minor'' var. ''vulgaris''. Richens sank as undifferentiated ''U. minor'' certain local English forms such as [[Ulmus minor 'Goodyeri'|''U. minor'' 'Goodyeri']], [[Ulmus minor 'Hunnybunii'|''U. minor'' 'Hunnybunii']], [[Ulmus minor 'Sowerbyi'|''U. minor'' 'Sowerbyi']], and [[Ulmus minor 'Coritana'|''U. minor'' 'Coritana']].<ref>Richens, R. H., 'Studies on ''Ulmus'' 1. The Range of Variation of East Anglian Elms', [https://archive.bsbi.org/Wats3p138.pdf ''Watsonia'' 3: 138–153 (1955); bsbi.org]</ref><ref name = Richens280>Richens, R. H., ''Elm'' (Cambridge, 1983), Ch.7 'Botanical classification', note 86, p.280</ref>

===Eurasia===
[[Augustine Henry|Henry]]'s [[Ulmus minor var. italica|''Ulmus nitens'' var. ''italica'']], 'Mediterranean Elm' (1913), distinguished by its 14 to 18 pairs of leaf-veins,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Elwes |first1=Henry John |last2=Henry |first2=Augustine |title=The Trees of Great Britain and Ireland, Volume VII |date=1913 |location=Edinburgh |isbn=978-1-108-06938-0 |page=1892–3 |url=https://archive.org/details/treesofgreatbrit07elweuoft/page/1892/mode/2up}}</ref> was accepted, despite the wide source-area claimed for it ("Italy, Spain, Portugal and Algeria"), as ''U. carpinifolia'' var. ''italica'' <small>Henry</small>, by [[Johann Gerd Krüssmann|Krüssman]] (1984), who included a photograph of a specimen in [[Gisselfeld|Gisselfeld Park]], Denmark.<ref>Krüssman, Gerd, ''Manual of Cultivated Broad-Leaved Trees & Shrubs'' (1984 vol. 3), pl.144</ref> [[William Jackson Bean|Bean]] (1988), however, considered it "a variety of rather dubious standing",<ref>[http://beanstreesandshrubs.org/browse/ulmus/ulmus-carpinifolia-gleditsch/ Bean, W. J., ''Trees and shrubs hardy in Great Britain'' (1988) beanstreesandshrubs.org]</ref> and it was ignored by Richens (1983).

[[Ulmus canescens|''U. canescens'']] <small>Melville</small> and ''[[Ulmus minor 'Boissieri'|U. boissieri]]'' <small>Grudz.</small> were both sunk as ''U. minor'' by Richens.<ref name=Richens1983>{{cite book |last= Richens|first=R.H. |date=1983 |title=Elm |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=0g49AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA279|publisher= Cambridge University Press|page=279 §82 |isbn=978-0-521-24916-4 }}</ref> The former is found throughout the eastern Mediterranean, including Palestine and Israel, and is distinguished by its leaves, densely downy on the underside when mature.<ref name=Melville,b>Melville, R. (1957). Ulmus canescens: an eastern Mediterranean elm. ''Kew Bulletin'': 499–502, 1957</ref><ref>[http://flora.org.il/en/plants/ULMMIN/ Flora of Israel and adjacent areas]</ref> The latter is a little-known tree found in Iran, in the Zagros forests and the Kerman / Kermanshah area.<ref name=Grudz.>{{cite journal |last1=Grudzinskaya |first1=I. A. |title=The new elm species - Ulmus boissieri. New species of Ulmaceae from Iran |journal=Botanicheskii Zhurnal |date=1977 |page=856 |volume=62 |issue=6 |publisher=Komarov Botanical Institute |location=St. Petersburg, Russia |url=http://en.arch.botjournal.ru/data/upload/botjournal_archive/ORIG/0005/0005313.pdf|language= ru|archive-url=https://archive.today/20230721193347/http://en.arch.botjournal.ru/data/upload/botjournal_archive/ORIG/0005/0005313.pdf|archive-date=21 July 2023|url-status=live}}</ref>
[[Peter Shaw Green|Green]] and Richens also sank [[Ulmus minor 'Suberosa'|''U. minor'' var. ''suberosa'']] <small>(Moench) Rehder</small> - the so-called 'Cork-barked elm', ''korkulme'' (Germany) or ''wiąz korkowa'' (Poland), as a genetically random, maritime or juvenile form of ''U. minor'', insufficiently differentiated to merit varietal status, its name a relic of taxonomic conservatism.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Green |first=Peter Shaw |author-link=Peter Shaw Green |date=1964 |title=Registration of cultivar names in Ulmus|url=https://archive.org/stream/arnoldiaarno_21#page/40/mode/2up/|journal=Arnoldia |volume=24|pages=41–80 |number=6–8 |publisher=[[Arnold Arboretum]], [[Harvard University]] |doi=10.5962/p.249479 |access-date=16 February 2017|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>Richens, R. H., ''Elm'' (Cambridge 1983), p.83, p. 278</ref>

==Hybrids==
The tree's natural range generously overlaps that of [[wych elm]] ''Ulmus glabra'' to the north, and readily hybridizes with it to produce the so-called 'Dutch elm' ''[[Ulmus × hollandica]]''.<ref>Richens, R. H., ''Elm'' (Cambridge, 1983), p. 95, 233</ref>

In Spain and Italy ''Ulmus minor'' has naturally hybridized with [[Siberian elm]] ''U. pumila''. In Spain ''U. pumila'' was introduced in the 16th century and has since spread widely, contributing to conservation concerns for ''U. minor''.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1046/j.1365-2540.2000.00740.x | pmid=11012718 | volume=85 | issue=2 | title=Identification of native and hybrid elms in Spain using isozyme gene markers | year=2000 | journal=Heredity | pages=157–166 | last1 = Miguel | doi-access=free | bibcode=2000Hered..85..157C }}</ref> In Italy ''U. pumila'' was introduced in the 1930s; research is ongoing into the extent of its hybridisation with ''U. minor''.<ref name="Brunet-et-al-2013">{{cite journal |last1=Brunet |first1=Johanne |last2=Zalapa |first2=Juan E. |last3=Pecori |first3=Francesco |last4=Santini |first4=Alberto |date=14 May 2013 |title=Hybridization and introgression between the exotic Siberian elm, ''Ulmus pumila'', and the native Field elm, ''U. minor'', in Italy |journal=Biol Invasions |volume=15 |issue=12 |pages=2717–2730 |doi=10.1007/s10530-013-0486-z |bibcode=2013BiInv..15.2717B |s2cid=14385250}}</ref> The resulting hybrid has not yet been given a formal botanical name, though there are cultivated forms such as [[Ulmus 'Recerta'|'Recerta']] and [[Ulmus 'Fiorente'|'Fiorente']] (see 'Hybrid cultivars').

*''[[Ulmus × hollandica]]''
*[[Ulmus davidiana var. japonica × U. minor|''Ulmus davidiana'' var. ''japonica'' × ''U. minor'']]
*[[Ulmus 'Androssowii'#Ulmus × androssowii|''U. minor'' × ''U. pumila'']]

==Hybrid cultivars==
''U. minor'' hybridises naturally with ''[[U. glabra]]'', producing elms of the ''[[Ulmus × hollandica]]'' group, from which there have arisen a number of cultivars:
{{#section:List of elm cultivars, hybrids and hybrid cultivars|Ulmus_x_hollandica_cultivars}}

The tree has featured strongly in artificial hybridization experiments in Europe and to a lesser extent in the United States. The hybrid [[Ulmus davidiana var. japonica × U. minor|''Ulmus davidiana'' var. ''japonica'' × ''U. minor'']] was raised at the [[Arnold Arboretum]] before 1924.<ref name = "MortonLivCollUlmus">[http://quercus.mortonarb.org/search.php?plantName=Ulmus&collectionCombo=&accessnbr= The Morton Arboretum Living Collection, ''Ulmus'' list, quercus.mortonarb.org]{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Most of the European research was based at [[Wageningen]] in the [[Netherlands]] until 1992, whence a number of hybrid cultivars have been commercially released since 1960. The earlier trees were raised in response to the initial [[Dutch elm disease]] pandemic that afflicted Europe after the [[First World War]], and were to prove vulnerable to the much more virulent strain of the disease that arrived in the late 1960s. However, further research eventually produced several trees highly resistant to disease which were released after 1989.<ref name=Heybroek,2>{{cite book|last1=Heybroek|first1=H.M.|editor1-last=Sticklen|editor1-first=Mariam B.|editor2-last=Sherald|editor2-first=James L.|title=Dutch Elm Disease Research|date=1993|publisher=Springer-Verlag|location=New York, USA|pages=16–25|access-date=26 October 2017|chapter=The Dutch Elm Breeding Program|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=avvxBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA16|isbn=978-1-4615-6874-2}}</ref>

*[[Ulmus 'Arno'|Arno]], [[Ulmus 'Clusius'|Clusius]], [[Ulmus 'Columella'|Columella]], [[Ulmus 'Commelin'|Commelin]], [[Ulmus 'Den Haag'|Den Haag]], [[Ulmus 'Fiorente'|Fiorente]], [[Ulmus 'Frontier'|Frontier]], [[Ulmus 'Fuente Umbria'|Fuente Umbria]], [[Ulmus 'Groeneveld'|Groeneveld]], [[Ulmus 'Homestead'|Homestead]], [[Ulmus 'Lobel'|Lobel]], [[Ulmus 'Nanguen' = Lutece|Nanguen = {{tdes|Lutèce|caps}}]], [[Ulmus × hollandica 'Pioneer'|Pioneer]], [[Ulmus 'Plantyn'|Plantyn]], [[Ulmus 'Plinio'|Plinio]], [[Ulmus 'Recerta'|Recerta]], [[Ulmus 'San Zanobi'|San Zanobi]], [[Ulmus 'Toledo'|Toledo]], [[Ulmus 'Urban'|Urban]], [[Ulmus 'Wanoux' = Vada|Wanoux = {{tdes|Vada|caps}}]]
